title: Diagnosing Sewer Gas, Vent Blockage, and Sagging Main Drain with Camera Inspection in a 60-Year-Old Home

locations.name: Behind the bathroom → main drain/vent stack area
locations.basis: Transcript identifies a drain, waste, and vent system located behind the bathroom and references main drain access.

summary: This Old House follows a diagnostic workflow for a bathroom that smells like sewer gas and exhibits abnormal water movement when fixtures upstream are used. A camera is run down the vent and then through a disguised main drain to assess the line. Observations reveal water in the drain where it should be dry, a possible house trap (rat trap) under the floor, and a pipe path that unexpectedly angles downward. Using a camera locator, the team pinpoints the location of the camera head and depth, then performs a water-level test to determine whether there is a restriction. The analysis leads to a sagged main drain with an aging cast-iron/lead joint system, suggesting the need to open the floor, replace the main line, remodel the bathroom, and address venting to prevent future sewer-gas issues.

sections.title: Symptom discovery and initial assessment
concepts: sudden sewer smell in bathroom
intermittent odor tied to fixture use
upstream toilet flush causes water level movement in the fixture
sections.description: Houseowners report a sewer odor in the bathroom and note that the water level in the toilet bounces when the upstairs toilet is flushed or the shower is used, suggesting a venting issue.

sections.title: Vent/ DWV system overview and initial camera steps
concepts: drain-waste-vent (DWV) system behind the bathroom
reference to a cleanout and the main drain path under the bathroom
upstairs fixtures affecting basement/ground-floor plumbing
sections.description: A plumber explains the DWV layout behind the bathroom and the role of the roof vent, setting up for a later camera inspection down the vent and the drain.

sections.title: Finding water in the drain and locating the trap hypothesis
concepts: water accumulation about 22 feet from the access
drain path not leading directly to the street; potential old line or alternate route
early speculation about a trap/obstruction near the access
sections.description: The team notes that water is present in the drain at a distance, which is abnormal for a drainage line that should be mostly dry, prompting further excavation and exploration.

sections.title: House trap concept and the need for access points
concepts: house trap (aka rat trap) in the system
why traps complicate snaking and cleaning
role of cleanouts and access in servicing the main line
sections.description: A PVC mockup introduces the house trap concept, explaining how a trap fills with water and blocks access to clear the line, and why cleanouts were historically used.

sections.title: Camera head locator demonstration and localization
concepts: drain camera locator detects camera head
magnetic poles mark the head and equator for depth and direction
measurements show the head is about 2 ft 8 in down
sections.description: The crew uses a locator to pinpoint the camera head, confirming the line direction and depth, and to determine where to dig for the trap.

sections.title: Water-level testing to diagnose obstruction vs. sag
concepts: flush test to see if trap or line obstructs flow
observing water level behavior during repeated flushes
evidence pointing toward a sagged pipe rather than a simple obstruction
sections.description: A toilet flush test is used to verify whether water in the line is obstructed; subsequent observations indicate the water level behavior is inconsistent with a simple obstruction, suggesting a sagging pipe.

sections.title: Diagnosis and proposed remediation: sag, venting, and remodel
concepts: pipe sag indicates movement of fittings and potential traps
aging cast-iron joints and sand under the bathroom area
solution: open the floor, replace the main drain, remodel bathroom, and address venting
possible removal/adjustment of the house trap to restore future accessibility
sections.description: The team concludes the main drain has sagged, creating a secondary trap and sewer-gas pathways; the recommended fix is a major repair: open the floor, replace the pipe, remodel the bathroom, and ensure proper venting and future access.
